definition: Dillon’s rule is a fundamental tenet of American municipal law. The rule originates from an opinion of Judge John F. Dillon in City of Clinton v. Cedar Rapids & Missouri River Railroad (1868). Dillon’s rule says that local governments have three types of powers:  Those granted in express words,  Those necessarily or fairly implied in or incident to the powers expressly granted, and  Those essential to the declared objects and purposes of the corporation, not simply convenient, but indispensable. Additionally, the rule states that if there is any reasonable doubt whether a power has been conferred on a local government, then the power has not been conferred. For more on Dillon's Rule see this document from the Nebraska Legislative Research Office on the Principles of Local Governance and this New Hampshire report comparing Dillon’s rule and home rule.
